stemBlocks.value: A prism, not drawn to scale, has cross section PQRST and length 20 cm. PQRST is made up of rectangle PQRT and a semicircle RST, with PQ = 6 cm and QR = 5 cm. Using π = 3.14, (i) calculate the area of the cross section PQRST. (Only part (i) appears in this extract.)
Think first: The cross section is a composite shape, so split it into the rectangle and the semicircle and add their areas.

solutionSteps.instruction: Find the area of rectangle PQRT.
Identify the diameter and radius of the semicircle.

contentBlocks.value: TR is opposite PQ in the rectangle, so TR = 6 cm and r = 6 / 2

solutionSteps.instruction: Find the area of the semicircle.

contentBlocks.value: ½ x π x r² = ½ x 3.14 x 3²= ½ x 3.14 x 9

strategyBlocks.value: Find the rectangle's area from PQ and QR, note that the semicircle's diameter equals TR = PQ = 6 cm so its radius is 3 cm, then add the two areas.

finalAnswerBlocks.value: (i) The area of the cross section PQRST is 44.13 cm².

whyThisWorks.value: Areas of non-overlapping parts add, so a composite figure can always be broken into shapes whose formulas you know. The semicircle sits on the side TR of the rectangle, and opposite sides of a rectangle are equal, which is what fixes its diameter at 6 cm without any extra measurement. Halving the full circle area gives the semicircle because a diameter divides a circle into two equal pieces.

commonErrors.misconception: Using 6 cm as the radius of the semicircle instead of the diameter.
commonErrors.correctiveNote: Avoid this: Using 6 cm as the radius of the semicircle instead of the diameter.

commonErrors.misconception: Using the full circle area and forgetting to halve it.

examTip.value: Mark the radius on the diagram as soon as you spot the circle. Half of every radius error in this topic starts with reading a diameter as a radius.
